summary: A best current practice that defines the administratively scoped IPv4 multicast space as 239.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255, with simple semantics for implementing it. It also provides a mapping to IPv6 multicast addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of addresses for group messages that stay inside one organization and never leave it.

questions: why not use ttl scoping for multicast
subtitle: Reserving 239.0.0.0/8 for multicast groups that stay inside administrative boundaries, instead of relying on TTL tricks.

tldr.problem: Multicast was scoped with TTL thresholds, which was hard to implement reliably, mixed with the TTL's job of limiting datagram lifetime, and could stop pruning from working.
tldr.mechanism: The IPv4 range 239.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 is defined as administratively scoped. Routers configured as boundaries do not forward packets for those addresses across an interface, and the addresses are locally assigned.
tldr.outcome: It gives clear semantics for scoped multicast, with a Local Scope at 239.255.0.0/16 and an Organization Local Scope at 239.192.0.0/14, but it is not a security mechanism.

today: RFC 2365 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 23) published in July 1998. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with TTL Scoping
sections.content:
Most multicast implementations of the time scoped traffic with the TTL field in the IP header. Operators on the MBONE engineered TTL thresholds so traffic stayed in some administratively defined region: a packet is not forwarded across an interface unless its remaining TTL is greater than the threshold.

RFC 2365 lists the weaknesses. The TTL is also used in its traditional role of limiting datagram lifetime, and these conflicting roles made TTL scoping difficult to implement reliably. A more serious problem is the interaction with broadcast and prune protocols such as DVMRP: the router that discards a packet cannot prune upstream sources, so it keeps sinking all multicast traffic whether or not there are downstream receivers. Sending prunes from the discard point could discard legitimate traffic, because later packets could take another path and arrive with a larger TTL.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling a message how many hops it may travel is like telling a paper plane how far to fly. It is hard to get right, and the plane still mixes up the people who are trying to stop it.

sections.title: The Administratively Scoped Space
sections.content:
Administratively scoped IP multicast offers two key properties. First, packets sent to administratively scoped addresses do not cross configured administrative boundaries. Second, these addresses are locally assigned, so they need not be unique across boundaries.

The administratively scoped IPv4 multicast space is defined as the range 239.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255.

To support it, a router should allow per-interface scoped multicast boundaries. Such a boundary router does not forward packets matching an interface's boundary definition in either direction, and the two-way check avoids problems on multi-access networks. It also always prunes the boundary for dense-mode groups and does not accept joins for sparse-mode groups in the administratively scoped range.
sections.plainLanguage: A block of addresses is set aside for private group chats. The doors of each neighborhood are told never to let those chats through in either direction.

sections.title: Local and Organization Local Scopes
sections.content:
The structure is loosely based on the IPv6 addressing architecture of RFC 1884. Two scopes are defined.

  • IPv4 Local Scope: 239.255.0.0/16. It is the minimal enclosing scope and is not further divisible. It must not span any other scope boundary, and must be completely contained within or equal to any larger scope. Where scope regions overlap, the overlap must be in its own local scope. It may later grow downward into 239.254.0.0/16 and 239.253.0.0/16, but those should not be used until the first range is no longer sufficient.
  • IPv4 Organization Local Scope: 239.192.0.0/14, the space from which an organization should allocate sub-ranges for private scopes. The ranges 239.0.0.0/10, 239.64.0.0/10 and 239.128.0.0/10 are unassigned and left available for expansion, in case later revisions define scopes larger than organizations.

Two other scope classes already exist: the statically assigned link-local scope 224.0.0.0/24 and global scope. The RFC lists existing global allocations such as 224.2.127.254 for SAPv1 announcements.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one small circle, the building, and one bigger circle, the whole company. The company circle is where you carve out your own rooms.

sections.title: Topological Requirements for Boundaries
sections.content:
A scoped region is a topological region with one or more boundary routers that share boundary definitions. Administrators may configure a scope whenever constrained scope is needed, and scopes may overlap. The limits are that a region must be connected (a path exists between any two nodes without leaving the region) and convex (no path between two points of the region can cross its boundary).

If scopes intersect topologically, the outer scope must consist of its address space minus the address spaces of any intersecting scopes. It is therefore recommended that topologically intersecting scopes should not intersect in address range. Every scope boundary is also a boundary for the Local Scope, so packets for 239.255.0.0/16 must not be forwarded across any link that has a scoped boundary defined.
sections.plainLanguage: A neighborhood must be one piece, with no road that leaves it and comes back in. If two neighborhoods overlap, they should not use the same house numbers.

sections.title: IPv6 Mapping and Relative Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC maps IPv4 prefixes to IPv6 scope values: link-local scope (value 2) is 224.0.0.0/24, the Local Scope is shown against value 3 as 239.255.0.0/16, organization-local scope (value 8) is 239.192.0.0/14, and global scope (value E) is 224.0.1.0-238.255.255.255.

The high-order /24 of every scoped region is reserved for relative assignments: an integer offset from the highest address in the scope. In the Local Scope, 239.255.255.0/24 is reserved for them. Relative assignment 0, address 239.255.255.255, exists for SAP, and assignment 1 is 239.255.255.254. The rest of the region is for dynamic assignment.

Requests for relative assignments go to IANA, advised by an area expert appointed by the relevant Area Director. They should be given only to services that cannot use a dynamic assignment protocol to find their address, such as a dynamic address assignment service itself. The RFC also says that a scope discovery protocol (MZAP) and an address allocation protocol would need to be developed to make scopes other than the Local Scope practical.
sections.plainLanguage: The last few addresses in each block are kept for the first signposts, such as the one that tells you where the other signs are.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Organizations should not rely on administratively scoped addresses to keep sensitive data inside. A boundary router that is mis-configured, has a bug in its scoping code, or has other problems could forward a scoped packet outside its proper scope, and the organization's data would leave.

Sensitive data should be protected with a confidentiality mechanism such as encryption, either as an application feature or at the IP layer with ESP. Manual key distribution might be feasible within a scoped group. The RFC also notes that the boundary router is not necessarily providing any firewall capability.
sections.plainLanguage: A door that is supposed to stay shut can still be left open by mistake. If a message is a secret, put it in a locked box anyway.
